A reusable split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the cam ring that advances the jaws is itself split, one segment travelling with each half of the frame, and is made into a working ring by the act of closing the frame.

The clamp has a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and joined at a latch end by a releasable latch, so that the frame halves can be swung apart, placed around a pipe that is already installed, and closed again. Three jaw carriages are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. Each jaw carriage is slidable in a radial guide of the frame and carries a jaw pad that is mounted on the jaw carriage for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface to the pipe. Because each jaw pad pivots, it bears on the pipe without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. The cam ring is segmented. A first cam-ring segment is carried by the first frame half and a second cam-ring segment is carried by the second frame half, so each segment stays with its own frame half when the clamp is opened. The first cam-ring segment and the second cam-ring segment have complementary drive faces at the hinge end and complementary drive faces at the latch end. Closing the frame halves brings those complementary drive faces into engagement and couples the cam-ring segments so that they move together as one cam ring about the pipe, and the faces separate again when the frame halves are swung apart.

Each jaw carriage carries a follower that is received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. The latch carries a wedge. Moving the latch drives the wedge against a ring drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled cam ring through a limited stroke about the pipe. The oblique slots are identical in inclination and are distributed circumferentially to match the jaw carriages, so that the common rotation of the cam ring produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage and the inward travel of the three jaw carriages is synchronized. A carriage spring biases each jaw carriage outward, so that releasing the latch retracts the jaw carriages and lifts the jaw pads off the pipe before the frame halves are opened.

The latch has a first position in which it holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which it drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. The two positions separate the act of capturing the pipe from the act of loading the jaws.

A force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive path between a latch handle of the latch and the wedge. Once all of the jaw pads have contacted the pipe, further travel of the latch handle toward the over-center position is absorbed by compression of the force-limiting spring stack instead of forcing one jaw pad farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack, and the clamping load is set by that spring stack rather than by the position at which the latch comes to rest.

An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing of the latch when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, so that the position of the indicator pin relative to that fixed edge reports mechanically that the clamp is loaded within the range. The indicator reports clamp loading and does not measure pipe diameter.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool or a conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages.

A method of clamping a pipe and a method of releasing the clamp are also disclosed, in which the frame halves are closed about the pipe to couple the cam-ring segments, the latch is moved to the first position and then to the over-center position to rotate the coupled cam ring, and the latch travel remaining after the jaw pads seat is taken up in the force-limiting spring stack.

Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations frequently has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports all have to be attached to a run of pipe that is already installed and often still in service. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.

A split frame creates a mechanical difficulty that a one piece collar does not have. The tightening motion has to be delivered across the split line. Where the two frame halves are drawn toward one another so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe, the closing force enters the frame at the split line, and the grip the pipe feels depends on the closure hardware and on where around the arc the pipe is touched. When the clamp is meant to hold a measuring head in a repeatable position, a grip that varies in that way is a source of error, and repeated opening and closing need not return the head to the same place.

Where the frame is instead fitted with individually adjustable jaws or screws that are wound in against the pipe one at a time, the grip is separated from the split line, but a tool is needed, the operator has to balance the jaws by feel, and the work is slow. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed off the axis of the frame, and the clamp is again seated differently each time it is fitted.

Clamps of both kinds are commonly sized for a nominal pipe diameter, so a technician has to carry a set of clamps and identify the correct one before working. A jaw face that is flat, or curved to one nominal diameter, meets a pipe of another diameter along an edge rather than over an area.

An operator working with a quick acting latch also has little to go on in judging how hard the clamp has been applied. A latch that snaps shut can feel much the same whether the jaws have seated properly on the pipe, whether the pipe is at the small end of the range and the jaws have barely reached it, or whether the mechanism has been travelled too far. Torque measurement is available for a bolted clamp but not for a latch, and a diameter reading indicates the size of the pipe rather than the load the clamp is carrying.

There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe of a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, and that reports mechanically when the clamping load has reached the intended range.

Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations frequently has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports all have to be attached to a run of pipe that is already installed and often still in service. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.

A split frame creates a mechanical difficulty that a one piece collar does not have. The tightening motion has to be delivered across the split line. The common answer is to draw the two frame halves toward one another, typically with a bolt, a toggle or a band, so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe. Because the closing force enters the frame at the split line, the grip is concentrated near the split and falls away around the arc, the frame is deformed in service, and the load carried by the clamp reacts back into the closure hardware. When the clamp is meant to hold a measuring head in a repeatable position, that uneven and closure dependent grip is a direct source of error, and repeated opening and closing does not return the head to the same place.

A second approach fits the frame with individually adjustable jaws or screws that are wound in against the pipe one at a time. That approach decouples the grip from the split line, but it requires a tool, it requires the operator to balance the jaws by feel, and it is slow. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed off the axis of the frame, thin walled pipe can be dented, and the clamp is again seated differently each time it is fitted.

Clamps of both kinds are also usually sized for a nominal pipe diameter, so a technician has to carry a set of clamps and identify the correct one before working. Flat or nominally curved jaw faces bear on a pipe of any other diameter along an edge rather than over an area.

Finally, an operator working with a quick acting latch has no reliable way of knowing how hard the clamp has been applied. A latch that snaps shut gives the same tactile feel whether the jaws have seated properly on the pipe, whether the pipe is at the small end of the range and the jaws have barely reached it, or whether the mechanism has been over travelled. Torque measurement is available for a bolted clamp but not for a latch, and a diameter reading indicates only the size of the pipe rather than the load the clamp is carrying.

There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe of a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, that does not take its grip from the split line, and that tells the operator mechanically when the clamping load has reached the intended range.

- An annular body drawn as concentric outer and inner boundary circles centered in the drawing area. The space between them is open, without hatching, and the region inside the inner circle is empty. No pipe is drawn.
- Within that space, a narrow band drawn as two concentric arcs set toward the outer boundary. This band is the cam ring, divided at two diametrically opposite locations, one left and one right, each division drawn as a short line across the width of the band.
- Outboard of the band, a channel outline of two further concentric arcs between the band and the outer circle, so the band sits in that channel, drawn in the three arc stretches between the slideways.
- Three slideways through the annular body at roughly equal angular intervals, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, none at either division. Each is a pair of parallel straight lines running radially between the two boundary circles.
- In each slideway a carriage drawn as a radially long rectangle, narrower than the slideway so the guide lines stay visible on both sides. Each carriage stops short of the inner circle and its outer end reaches the band.
- On the inner end of each carriage a pad drawn as a small block whose inner edge is a concave arc curving away from the center of the view, joined to the carriage at a small circle.
- At the outer end of each carriage a small circle representing a follower, lying on the band, and around it a slot drawn as an elongated closed outline through the band, inclined so its long direction is neither purely radial nor purely along the band. The three slots share one rotational sense.
- In the outer stretch of each slideway, between the carriage and the outer circle, a spring drawn as a short zigzag line.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.

A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.

The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.

To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. The disclosed essential relationship is that closure couples the ring segments and latch travel drives the coupled ring, while the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel.

- **[minor] Claim 9 recites "the distribution of the jaw carriages" without antecedent basis** (draft/09-claims.md claim 9) - Claim 1 recites that the jaw carriages are "distributed circumferentially about the frame" but never introduces "a distribution", so the definite article in claim 9 has no antecedent. The description has the same wording, so the fix is available in both places.

  - Suggested fix: Delete that clause, leaving "The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20."

1	In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when the clamp is closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be applied to a pipe 20 that is already installed and that cannot be entered from a free end.
6	
7	The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 may be machined, cast, molded or fabricated from metal or from a reinforced polymer, the material being chosen for the service environment. The hinge 16 may be a pin hinge, a pair of interleaved knuckles on a common pin, or a flexible hinge section integral with the frame, provided that it holds the frame halves in register when they are closed. Closure of the frame halves in register is relied upon by the cam drive described below, so the hinge 16 and the releasable latch 18 are arranged to bring the two frame halves to a repeatable closed position rather than merely to hold them near one another.
8	
9	A plurality of jaw carriages 22 is distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. In the form shown in FIG. 1 the plurality of jaw carriages 22 consists of three jaw carriages 22 distributed about the closed frame. Three carriages define a stable seat on a round pipe without over constraining it. The synchronizing relationship described below is not limited to that number, and a clamp having more than three jaw carriages 22 is built in the same way, each additional jaw carriage 22 being coupled to the cam ring by its own follower and its own oblique slot as described below.
10	
11	The frame carries a mounting boss 66, which stands radially outside the cam drive described below. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10 and may be a threaded pad, a dovetail, a flange with fastener holes, or any other fitting suitable for the item to be carried. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22. A load applied to the mounting boss 66 is therefore reacted through the frame and into the jaw pads, and is not carried by the cam drive, so a moment applied by a carried instrument does not disturb the setting of the jaws.
12	
13	Jaw carriages and jaw pads
14	
15	Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 may be a rectangular slideway, a pair of parallel rails, or a bore that receives a cylindrical shank of the jaw carriage 22, and it constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame. In the illustrated form two of the radial guides 24 are formed in one of the frame halves and a remaining one of the radial guides 24 is formed in the other frame half, so that each frame half carries at least one jaw carriage 22 and each frame half is loaded by the clamping action.
16	
17	Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement about a pad axis and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the concave bearing surface aligns itself with the surface of the pipe 20 that it meets, and bears on the pipe over an area rather than along an edge. The split pipe clamp 10 therefore grips pipes over a range of diameters and does not require a tool specific pipe diameter. The pad axis is parallel to the axis of the pipe 20 in the illustrated form, and the jaw pad 26 may be faced with an elastomer, with a soft metal, or with a friction material where the pipe surface is to be protected.
18	
19	A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. The carriage spring 42 may be a compression spring seated in the radial guide 24, a tension spring acting between the jaw carriage 22 and the frame, or a leaf element. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 and lift the jaw pads 26 clear of the pipe 20, so that the frame halves can be swung apart without the jaw pads 26 dragging on the pipe.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring
22	
23	A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 is an annular channel of the frame, concentric with the central axis of the closed frame, that locates the cam ring 30 radially and axially while allowing it to rotate through a limited stroke about that axis. Because the annular guide 36 continues around both frame halves, the reaction to the clamping load is taken by the frame around the whole arc rather than across the split line between the frame halves.
24	
25	The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame radially outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.
26	
27	The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung fully apart without dismantling the drive.
28	
29	The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.
30	
31	The complementary drive faces may be plain abutment faces lying in radial planes, faces inclined so that one segment end laps the other, or a tongue on one segment received in a recess of the other. What matters is that in the closed frame each pair of faces transmits circumferential drive from one segment to the other in the direction of the clamping stroke, and that the faces separate freely when the frame halves are swung apart. The coupling is made by the closing motion of the frame halves themselves, so no fastener, key or separate coupling action is required of the operator, and there is no state in which the frame is closed but the drive is not yet made up.
32	
33	Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. The follower 40 may be a pin, a roller on a pin, or a block. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are identical in inclination and are distributed to match the distribution of the jaw carriages 22, so that a single rotation of the cam ring 30 produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. Advance of the jaws is therefore synchronized by the geometry of the oblique slots 38 rather than by successive adjustment of individual jaws, and no jaw can be advanced independently of the others.
34	
35	Where the pipe 20 is not exactly centered when the frame is closed, the jaw pad 26 that reaches the pipe first begins to center the pipe within the frame, because the other jaw pads 26 continue to advance by the same amount until they too make contact. The inclination of the oblique slots 38 may be chosen to trade stroke against mechanical advantage, a shallower inclination giving a larger clamping force for a given drive force and a smaller radial travel for a given rotation, and the useful range of pipe diameters for a given clamp is set by the total radial travel available at the jaw carriages 22.
36	
37	The latch drive
38	
39	The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke. The ring drive face 54 is presented at the latch end of the cam ring 30 and is inclined to the path of the wedge 52, so that advance of the wedge 52 is converted into circumferential displacement of the cam ring 30. The ring drive face 54 may be formed on a lug that projects outwardly from one of the cam-ring segments at the latch end, or on the end of a segment itself where the annular guide 36 is open to the wedge 52. The limited stroke is bounded by the frame, by the ends of the oblique slots 38, or by a stop face of the annular guide 36, so that the cam ring 30 cannot be driven beyond the working range of the jaw carriages 22.
40	
41	The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 closed around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20, the cam ring 30 standing at the beginning of its stroke and the jaw carriages 22 remaining retracted under the carriage springs 42. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20, and in which the line of action of the clamping load passes over the pivot of the releasable latch 18 so that the load holds the latch closed rather than opening it. The first position allows the operator to capture the pipe 20 and slide or rotate the split pipe clamp 10 to its intended station before any clamping load is applied.
42	
43	Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58, a force-limiting spring stack 62 and an over-center link 68. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52, and the over-center link 68 connects the latch handle 56 to the force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 may be a stack of disc springs, a nest of helical compression springs, or a single compression spring, selected to a chosen preload and rate.
44	
45	Until all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, the force-limiting spring stack 62 transmits the drive from the latch handle 56 to the wedge 52 substantially without compressing, because the resistance of the carriage springs 42 is small compared with the preload of the force-limiting spring stack 62. Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The additional latch travel that remains after contact, which varies from installation to installation with the diameter and the tolerance of the pipe 20, is therefore taken up elastically. The clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 and not by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest, so the same clamp applies a comparable load to a large pipe and to a small pipe within its range, and a thin walled pipe is not deformed by the surplus travel of the latch.
46	
47	An indicator pin 64 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 62 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 64 is carried by the movable end of the force-limiting spring stack 62 and projects through an opening of the latch housing 58, so that its position relative to the fixed edge 60 follows the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 62. The predetermined compression range corresponds to the intended clamping load of the split pipe clamp 10, and the emergence of the indicator pin 64 past the fixed edge 60 is a visible mechanical report that the clamp is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20. No electrical power, instrumentation or calibration equipment is required at the pipe to read it, and the report is available at the moment the latch is closed.
48	
49	Installation and removal
50	
51	To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping, and positions the split pipe clamp 10 along the pipe 20. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Remaining travel of the latch handle 56 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator confirms the clamping load by observing the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.
52	
53	To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 54, and the carriage springs 42 rotate the cam ring 30 back through the oblique slots 38 and retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable and may be fitted, removed and refitted without tools.
54	
55	The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.
56

The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping, and positions the split pipe clamp 10 along the pipe 20. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Remaining travel of the latch handle 56 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator confirms the clamping load by observing the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 54, and the carriage springs 42 rotate the cam ring 30 back through the oblique slots 38 and retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable and may be fitted, removed and refitted without tools.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

The clamp has a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and joined at a latch end by a releasable latch, so that the frame halves can be swung apart, placed around a pipe that is already installed, and closed again. A plurality of jaw carriages is distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. Each jaw carriage is slidable in a radial guide of the frame and carries a jaw pad that is mounted on the jaw carriage for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface to the pipe. Because each jaw pad pivots, it seats itself on the pipe surface it meets, and the clamp is not restricted to one nominal pipe diameter.

A cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. The cam ring is segmented. A first cam-ring segment is carried by the first frame half and a second cam-ring segment is carried by the second frame half, so each segment stays with its own frame half when the clamp is opened. The first cam-ring segment and the second cam-ring segment have complementary drive faces at the hinge end and complementary drive faces at the latch end. Closing the frame halves brings those complementary drive faces into engagement and couples the cam-ring segments so that they move together as one cam ring about the pipe. Closure of the frame is therefore what creates the drive train, and no separate coupling step is asked of the operator.

Each jaw carriage carries a follower that is received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. The latch carries a wedge. Moving the latch drives the wedge against a ring drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled cam ring through a limited stroke about the pipe. Each oblique slot converts that common rotation into inward travel of its own jaw carriage, so that all of the jaw carriages advance together by an amount fixed by the geometry of the slots rather than by the judgment of the operator. A carriage spring biases each jaw carriage outward, so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws before the frame halves are opened. The clamping load is taken by the cam ring in the annular guide rather than across the split line, and the latch is not asked to hold the working load through the frame joint.

The latch has a first position in which it holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which it drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. The two positions separate the act of capturing the pipe from the act of loading the jaws, so the operator can position the clamp along the pipe while the frame is already captive.

A force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive path between a latch handle of the latch and the wedge. Once all of the jaw pads have contacted the pipe, further travel of the latch handle to the over-center position is absorbed by compression of the force-limiting spring stack instead of forcing one jaw farther than the others. The remaining latch travel is therefore taken up by a defined elastic element, the clamping load is bounded by that element, and a pipe that sits anywhere within the range of the clamp is gripped by a load set by the spring stack rather than by where the latch happens to reach its stop.

An indicator pin coupled to the force-limiting spring stack moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing of the latch when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a visible mechanical report that the clamp is loaded within that range. content.content:
1	Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations frequently has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports all have to be attached to a run of pipe that is already installed and often still in service. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.
2	
3	A split frame creates a mechanical difficulty that a one piece collar does not have. The tightening motion has to be delivered across the split line. The common answer is to draw the two frame halves toward one another, typically with a bolt, a toggle or a band, so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe. Because the closing force enters the frame at the split line, the grip is concentrated near the split and falls away around the arc, the frame is deformed in service, and the load carried by the clamp reacts back into the closure hardware. When the clamp is meant to hold a measuring head in a repeatable position, that uneven and closure dependent grip is a direct source of error, and repeated opening and closing does not return the head to the same place.
4	
5	A second approach fits the frame with individually adjustable jaws or screws that are wound in against the pipe one at a time. That approach decouples the grip from the split line, but it requires a tool, it requires the operator to balance the jaws by feel, and it is slow. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed off the axis of the frame, thin walled pipe can be dented, and the clamp is again seated differently each time it is fitted.
6	
7	Clamps of both kinds are also usually sized for a nominal pipe diameter, so a technician has to carry a set of clamps and identify the correct one before working. Flat or nominally curved jaw faces bear on a pipe of any other diameter along an edge rather than over an area.
8	
9	Finally, an operator working with a quick acting latch has no reliable way of knowing how hard the clamp has been applied. A latch that snaps shut gives the same tactile feel whether the jaws have seated properly on the pipe, whether the pipe is at the small end of the range and the jaws have barely reached it, or whether the mechanism has been over travelled. Torque measurement is available for a bolted clamp but not for a latch, and a diameter reading indicates only the size of the pipe rather than the load the clamp is carrying.
10	
11	There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe of a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, that does not take its grip from the split line, and that tells the operator mechanically when the clamping load has reached the intended range.
12

content.content:
1	A reusable split pipe clamp has two frame halves joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other, so the frame opens around a pipe already in place. Jaw carriages slide in radial guides and carry pivoting concave jaw pads. A segmented cam ring sits in an annular guide, one segment traveling with each frame half, and complementary drive faces at the hinge end and the latch end couple the segments into one rotating ring when the frame closes. A wedge on the latch turns the coupled ring through a limited stroke against a ring drive face, and oblique slots acting on followers advance the jaw carriages inward together. A force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs remaining latch travel, and an indicator pin moving past a fixed edge of the latch housing reports clamping load.

In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when the clamp is closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be applied to a pipe 20 transversely rather than being passed over an end of the pipe 20. When the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20, the split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 form an installed clamp assembly.

A plurality of jaw carriages 22 is distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. In the form shown in FIG. 1 the plurality of jaw carriages 22 consists of three jaw carriages 22 distributed about the closed frame.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66, which stands radially outside the cam drive described below. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the concave bearing surface aligns itself with the surface of the pipe 20 that it meets. The split pipe clamp 10 therefore grips pipes over a range of diameters and does not require a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 and lift the jaw pads 26 clear of the pipe 20, so that the frame halves can be swung apart without the jaw pads 26 dragging on the pipe.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 extends around the frame, concentric with the central axis of the closed frame, and retains the cam ring 30 while allowing it to rotate through a limited stroke about that axis.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame radially outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung fully apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame, each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one segment to the other in the direction of the clamping stroke, and the faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart. The coupling of the cam-ring segments is accordingly made by the closing motion of the frame halves themselves.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are identical in inclination and are distributed circumferentially to match the jaw carriages 22, so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the jaw carriages 22 is therefore synchronized by the geometry of the oblique slots 38 acting on the followers 40 of a single coupled cam ring 30, rather than by separate adjustment of each jaw.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 closed around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20, the cam ring 30 standing at the beginning of its stroke and the jaw carriages 22 remaining retracted under the carriage springs 42. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The additional latch travel that remains after contact, which varies from installation to installation with the diameter and the tolerance of the pipe 20, is therefore taken up elastically. The clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 and not by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest.

An indicator pin 64 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 62 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range corresponds to the intended clamping load of the split pipe clamp 10, and the position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a visible mechanical report that the clamp is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20. The report is mechanical, so no electrical power or instrumentation is required at the pipe 20 to read it, and the report is available at the moment the latch is closed.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Remaining travel of the latch handle 56 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator confirms the clamping load by observing the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable and may be fitted, removed and refitted without tools.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be applied to a pipe 20 that is already installed and that cannot be entered from a free end. The split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 together form an installed clamp assembly when the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20.

Three jaw carriages 22 are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame, as shown in FIG. 1.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 is an annular channel of the frame, concentric with the central axis of the closed frame, that retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about that axis.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are identical in inclination and are distributed circumferentially to match the jaw carriages 22, so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest.

An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

A reusable split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the ring that drives the jaws is itself split, one segment traveling with each half of the frame, and is made into a working ring by the act of closing the frame.

The clamp has a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and joined at a latch end by a releasable latch, so that the frame halves can be swung apart, placed around a pipe, and closed again. Three jaw carriages are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. Each jaw carriage is slidable in a radial guide of the frame and carries a jaw pad that is mounted on the jaw carriage for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface to the pipe. Because each jaw pad pivots, it bears on the pipe without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. The cam ring is segmented. A first cam-ring segment is carried by the first frame half and a second cam-ring segment is carried by the second frame half, so each segment stays with its own frame half when the clamp is opened. The first cam-ring segment and the second cam-ring segment have complementary drive faces at the hinge end and complementary drive faces at the latch end. Closing the frame halves brings those complementary drive faces into engagement and couples the cam-ring segments so that they move together as one cam ring about the pipe.

Each jaw carriage carries a follower that is received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. The latch carries a wedge. Moving the latch drives the wedge against a ring drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled cam ring through a limited stroke about the pipe. Each oblique slot converts that common rotation into inward travel of its own jaw carriage, so that all of the jaw carriages advance together by an amount fixed by the geometry of the slots rather than by separate adjustment of each jaw. A carriage spring biases each jaw carriage outward, so that releasing the latch retracts the jaw carriages and lifts the jaw pads off the pipe before the frame halves are opened.

The latch has a first position in which it holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which it drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. The two positions separate the act of capturing the pipe from the act of loading the jaws.

A force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive path between a latch handle of the latch and the wedge. Once all of the jaw pads have contacted the pipe, further movement of the latch handle toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack rather than forcing one jaw pad farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack, and the clamping load is set by that spring stack rather than by the position at which the latch comes to rest.

An indicator pin is visible on the latch and moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing of the latch when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report that the clamp is loaded within that range. The indicator reports clamp loading and does not measure pipe diameter.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool or a conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages.

A method of clamping a pipe and a method of releasing the clamp are also disclosed, in which the frame halves are closed about the pipe to couple the cam-ring segments, the latch is moved to the first position and then to the over-center position to rotate the coupled cam ring, and the latch travel that remains after the jaw pads seat is taken up by the force-limiting spring stack.

Each jaw carriage is slidable in a radial guide of the frame and carries a jaw pad that is mounted on the jaw carriage for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface to the pipe. Because each jaw pad pivots, it seats itself on the pipe surface it meets, and the clamp is not restricted to one nominal pipe diameter.

A cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. The cam ring is segmented. A first cam-ring segment is carried by the first frame half and a second cam-ring segment is carried by the second frame half, so each segment stays with its own frame half when the clamp is opened. The first cam-ring segment and the second cam-ring segment have complementary drive faces at the hinge end and complementary drive faces at the latch end. Closing the frame halves brings those complementary drive faces into engagement and couples the cam-ring segments so that they move together as one cam ring about the pipe. Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations often has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports are attached to a run of pipe that is already installed. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.

A split frame presents a mechanical problem that a one piece collar does not have, because the tightening motion has to be delivered to a frame that is divided. Where the grip is obtained by drawing the two frame halves toward one another so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe, the closing force enters the frame at the split line, and the grip that results depends on the closure hardware and on how far the halves have been drawn together.

Where instead the frame is fitted with jaws that are advanced against the pipe one at a time, the grip is taken away from the split line, but the jaws have to be balanced against one another by the operator. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed away from the axis of the frame, and the clamp is seated differently each time it is fitted.

A clamp whose jaw faces match one nominal pipe diameter also obliges a technician to select the clamp to suit the pipe before working, and a jaw face of fixed curvature meets a pipe of a different diameter along an edge rather than over an area.

An operator working with a quick acting latch further has little indication of how hard the clamp has been applied. The latch closes to the same position whether the jaws have only just reached the pipe or have been driven hard against it, so the feel of the latch does not report the load the clamp is carrying, and a reading of pipe diameter reports only the size of the pipe.

There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe over a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, and that reports mechanically to the operator when the clamping load has reached the intended range.

input.summary: The application now reads as one finished draft of the split pipe clamp: 17 claims in three statutory classes (clamp, installed clamp assembly, method), a description carrying only what the inventor disclosed, four figure briefs whose numeral declarations and sheet lists agree, and a numeral table of 28 numerals every one of which is used in the description and appears on a sheet. This turn I brought the Summary, Background, abstract, numeral table and claim ladder into line with the description, which had already been stripped of the candidate-introduced structure the reviewer identified. Specifically: the Summary's assertions that the grip is taken around the whole arc rather than across the split line, that the latch does not hold the working load, that the operator can station the clamp along the pipe in the first latch position, that no separate coupling step is asked of the operator, and that a load on the mounting boss cannot disturb the cam drive are all gone, because none of them appears in the inventor's material. structured_output.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there was nothing to read, nothing to cite and no reference vocabulary to steer around. The draft therefore contains no [REF:...] citation, and the Background makes no statement about any identified document. Because no art was supplied, I could not point to a reference that a given limitation clears. Instead I made claim 1 turn on the relationship the inventor calls essential and which is the least likely to be met by a general-purpose pipe clamp: the drive ring is divided into one segment per frame half, each segment stays with its own half when the clamp is opened, and closing the halves brings complementary drive faces into engagement at both the hinge end and the latch end so that the two segments rotate as one ring. The drive train exists only when the frame is closed, and the wedge on the latch then rotates that reassembled ring through a limited stroke while oblique slots convert the single rotation into common inward travel at every carriage, with a force-limiting spring stack in the drive path taking up the latch travel left over after the pads touch down. A conventional split clamp tightens by pulling its halves together across the split line, and a one-piece scroll or cam chuck cannot be opened around an installed pipe; the recited combination is neither. The specification states the technical problems these features answer, the divided frame that must nonetheless carry a continuous drive and the variable residual latch travel that would otherwise be forced into one jaw, so the argument material is in the document before it is needed. tool_use_result.originalFile:
In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be applied to a pipe 20 that is already installed and that cannot be entered from a free end. The split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 together form an installed clamp assembly when the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20.

Three jaw carriages 22 are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame, as shown in FIG. 1.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 is an annular channel of the frame, concentric with the central axis of the closed frame, that retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about that axis.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are identical in inclination and are distributed circumferentially to match the jaw carriages 22, so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest.

An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.
